title: III. The Second Marriage And The Second Family
section: Book I — The History Of A Family
paragraphs: Very shortly after getting his four-year-old Mitya off his hands, Fyodor Pavlovitch married a second time. This second marriage lasted eight years. He took this second wife, Sofya Ivanovna, also a very young girl, from another province, where he'd gone on some small piece of business together with a Jewish associate. Though Fyodor Pavlovitch was a drunkard and a vicious debauchee, he never once neglected investing his capital, and he managed his business affairs very successfully—though not, admittedly, very scrupulously. Sofya Ivanovna was the daughter of an obscure deacon, and was left an orphan from childhood, without relatives. She grew up in the household of a general's widow, a wealthy old lady of good standing who was at once her benefactress and her tormentor. I don't know the details, but I've heard that the orphan girl, a meek and gentle creature, was once cut down from a noose she'd hung from a nail in the attic—so unbearable were her sufferings from the whims and endless nagging of this old woman, who wasn't at heart bad-natured but had become an insufferable tyrant out of sheer idleness.

Fyodor Pavlovitch proposed to her; inquiries were made about him, and he was turned down. But again, as with his first marriage, he suggested an elopement to the orphan girl. There's very little doubt she'd never have married him at all if she'd known a bit more about him in time. But she lived in another province, and besides, what could a sixteen-year-old girl know, except that she'd be better off at the bottom of the river than staying with her benefactress? So the poor child traded a benefactress for a benefactor. This time Fyodor Pavlovitch didn't get a penny, since the general's widow was furious. She gave them nothing and cursed them both. But he hadn't been counting on a dowry; what drew him was the girl's remarkable beauty, above all her innocent look, which had a particular appeal for a depraved libertine who up to then had admired only the coarser kinds of feminine beauty.

“Those innocent eyes slit my soul up like a razor,” he used to say afterward, with his revolting snigger. In a man so depraved this might, of course, mean nothing more than a sensual attraction. Since he'd gotten no dowry with his wife, and had, so to speak, taken her “off the noose,” he didn't stand on ceremony with her. Making her feel that she'd “wronged” him, he took advantage of her extraordinary meekness and submissiveness to trample on the most basic decencies of marriage. He gathered loose women into his house and carried on drunken orgies right in front of his wife. To show what things had come to, I might mention that Grigory—the gloomy, stubborn, argumentative servant who had always hated his first mistress, Adelaïda Ivanovna—took the side of his new one. He championed her cause, cursing out Fyodor Pavlovitch in a manner hardly fitting for a servant, and on one occasion broke up the revels and drove all the disorderly women out of the house. In the end, this unhappy young woman, terrorized since childhood, fell into the kind of nervous illness most often found in peasant women said to be “possessed by devils.” At times, after terrible fits of hysterics, she even lost her mind. And yet she bore Fyodor Pavlovitch two sons, Ivan and Alexey—the eldest in the first year of the marriage, the second three years later. When she died, little Alexey was in his fourth year, and, strange as it seems, I know that he remembered his mother his whole life—like a dream, of course. When she died, almost exactly the same thing happened to the two little boys as had happened to their elder brother, Mitya. They were completely forgotten and abandoned by their father. They too were looked after by Grigory, and lived in his cottage, where they were found by the tyrannical old lady who had raised their mother. She was still alive, and hadn't, in all those eight years, forgotten the insult done to her. The whole time she had kept herself exactly informed of Sofya's way of life, and hearing of her illness and her hideous surroundings, she declared aloud two or three times to her servants:
“It serves her right. God has punished her for her ingratitude.”

Exactly three months after Sofya Ivanovna's death, the general's widow suddenly turned up in our town and went straight to Fyodor Pavlovitch's house. She spent only half an hour in town, but she got a great deal done. It was evening. Fyodor Pavlovitch, whom she hadn't seen in those eight years, came in to meet her drunk. The story goes that, the moment she saw him, without a word of explanation, she gave him two good, resounding slaps across the face, seized him by a tuft of hair, and shook him up and down three times. Then, without a word, she went straight to the cottage where the two boys were. Seeing at a glance that they were unwashed and in dirty linen, she promptly boxed Grigory's ears too, and, announcing that she would take both children away with her, wrapped them just as they were in a blanket, put them in her carriage, and drove off to her own town. Grigory took the blow like a devoted servant, without a word, and when he escorted the old lady to her carriage he gave her a low bow and solemnly declared that “God would repay her for the orphans.” “You're a blockhead all the same,” the old lady shouted back at him as she drove away.

Thinking it over, Fyodor Pavlovitch decided this was all for the best, and didn't refuse the general's widow his formal consent to whatever she proposed regarding his children's education. As for the slaps she'd given him, he drove all over town telling the story.

It happened that the old lady died soon after this, but she left the boys a thousand roubles each in her will, “for their education, and to be spent on them exclusively, on condition that it be so allotted as to last until they turn twenty-one, since it is more than adequate provision for such children. If other people see fit to throw their money away, let them.” I haven't read the will myself, but I've heard it was worded oddly in places, very whimsically. The main heir, Yefim Petrovitch Polenov, the provincial Marshal of Nobility, turned out, however, to be an honest man. Writing to Fyodor Pavlovitch, and seeing at once that nothing could be extracted from him for his children's education (though the man never directly refused, but simply stalled, as he always did in such cases, and was even at times gushingly sentimental about it), Yefim Petrovitch took a personal interest in the orphans. He grew especially fond of the younger one, Alexey, who lived for a long while as one of his own family. I ask the reader to note this from the start. To Yefim Petrovitch—a man of a generosity and humanity rarely met with—the young men owed more for their upbringing and education than to anyone else. He kept the two thousand roubles left to them by the general's widow intact, so that by the time they came of age their shares had doubled through accumulated interest. He educated both of them at his own expense, and certainly spent far more than a thousand roubles on each. I won't give a detailed account of their boyhood and youth here, but will mention only a few of the most important events. Of the elder, Ivan, I'll only say that he grew into a somewhat morose, withdrawn boy, though far from timid. By the age of ten he'd already realized that they were living not in their own home but on other people's charity, and that their father was a man it was shameful even to speak of. This boy began very early—almost in infancy, they say—to show a brilliant and unusual gift for learning. I don't know exactly why, but he left Yefim Petrovitch's household when he was barely thirteen, entering a Moscow gymnasium and boarding with an experienced, well-known teacher, an old friend of Yefim Petrovitch's. Ivan used to claim afterward that all this was due to Yefim Petrovitch's “zeal for good works,” who was taken with the idea that the boy's genius ought to be trained by a teacher of genius. But by the time the young man finished at the gymnasium and entered the university, neither Yefim Petrovitch nor that teacher was still alive. Since Yefim Petrovitch had made no arrangement for paying out the tyrannical old lady's legacy, which had by then grown from one thousand to two, it was held up by the usual bureaucratic delays inevitable in Russia, and the young man found himself in serious straits during his first two years at the university, forced to support himself the whole time he was studying. It should be noted that he made no attempt to contact his father—whether out of pride, or contempt for him, or simply his cool common sense telling him he'd get no real help from such a father. Whatever the case, the young man didn't despair in the slightest, and managed to find work, at first giving lessons at sixpence a time, then getting paragraphs about street incidents placed in the newspapers under the byline “Eye-Witness.” These pieces, it was said, were so lively and sharp that they were soon in demand. This alone showed the young man's practical and intellectual superiority over the crowds of needy, luckless students of both sexes who hang about newspaper and magazine offices, unable to come up with anything better than endless pleading for copying work or French translations. Once he'd gotten in with the editors, Ivan Fyodorovitch kept up the connection, and in his final years at the university he published brilliant reviews of books on various specialist subjects, so that he became known in literary circles. But it was only in his last year that he suddenly succeeded in catching the attention of a much wider circle of readers, so that a great many people noticed and remembered his name. It was a rather curious episode. Just as he'd left the university and was preparing to go abroad on his two thousand roubles, Ivan Fyodorovitch published, in one of the leading journals, a strange article that attracted general notice—on a subject he might have been assumed to know nothing about, since he was a student of natural science. The article dealt with a question being debated everywhere at the time: the position of the ecclesiastical courts. After running through several existing opinions on the subject, he went on to set out his own view. What was most striking about the article was its tone, and its unexpected conclusion. Many in the Church party took him unquestioningly for one of their own. And yet not only the secularists but even the atheists joined in applauding him. In the end some shrewd observers concluded that the article was nothing but an impudent, satirical piece of burlesque. I mention this episode in particular because the article found its way into our famous local monastery, where the monks, being especially interested in the question of ecclesiastical courts, were left thoroughly baffled by it. Learning the author's name, they took an interest in the fact that he was a native of the town, and the son of “that Fyodor Pavlovitch.” And it was just then that the author himself turned up among us.

Why Ivan Fyodorovitch had come to us I remember asking myself at the time, with a certain unease. This fateful visit, which would set off so many consequences, I never fully explained to myself. It seemed odd, on the face of it, that a young man so learned, so proud, and apparently so cautious, would suddenly turn up at such an infamous household, at the home of a father who had ignored him his whole life, barely knew him, never gave him a thought, and would never under any circumstances have given him money—though he was always afraid his sons Ivan and Alexey would come asking him for some. And here was the young man staying in the house of such a father, having lived with him for two months already, on the best of terms. This last fact was a particular source of wonder to many others besides me. Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, whom we've already mentioned, the cousin of Fyodor Pavlovitch's first wife, happened to be in the district again, visiting his estate. He'd come from Paris, which was his permanent home. I remember he was more surprised than anyone when he made the young man's acquaintance—Ivan interested him enormously, and Miüsov sometimes argued with him and, not without a pang, compared himself against him in terms of learning.

“He's proud,” he used to say, “he'll never be short of money; he's got enough to go abroad right now. What does he want here? Anyone can see he hasn't come for the money, since his father would never give him any. He has no taste for drink or dissipation, and yet his father can't do without him. The two of them get along so well!”

That was the truth: the young man clearly had influence over his father, who genuinely seemed to be behaving more decently, and even at times seemed ready to obey his son—though often extremely, even spitefully, contrary.

It was only later that we learned Ivan had come partly at the request, and in the interests, of his elder brother Dmitri, whom he was seeing for the first time on this very visit, though he'd been in correspondence with him before leaving Moscow about an important matter that concerned Dmitri more than himself. What that matter was, the reader will learn fully in due course. Yet even once I knew of this particular circumstance, I still found Ivan Fyodorovitch an enigmatic figure, and thought his visit rather mysterious.

I might add that Ivan appeared, at the time, in the role of mediator between his father and his elder brother Dmitri, who was in open conflict with his father and even planning to bring a lawsuit against him.

The family, I repeat, was now gathered together for the first time, and some of its members were meeting one another for the first time in their lives. The younger brother, Alexey, had already been among us for a year, having been the first of the three to arrive. It's of this brother, Alexey, that I find it hardest to speak in this introduction. And yet I must give some preliminary account of him, if only to explain one odd fact—that I have to introduce my hero to the reader wearing the cassock of a novice. Yes, he'd spent the last year in our monastery, and seemed prepared to be cloistered there for the rest of his life.
